keyVerseText: Philip, and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the publican; James the son of Alphaeus, and Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus;
rootMeaning: The name Θαδδαῖος (Thaddaîos) is of uncertain origin, with no clear etymological root provided in the available data. Its core sense is tied directly to the personal name Thaddaeus, which identifies a specific individual rather than conveying a descriptive meaning. This lack of a known root means the name functions primarily as a proper noun, distinguishing one of the apostles rather than offering a literal or symbolic meaning beyond that identification.
usageInScripture: The word Θαδδαῖος appears only twice in Scripture, both times referring to the same person, the apostle Thaddaeus. It is consistently translated as 'Thaddaeus,' indicating a proper name without variation or metaphorical extension. This consistency underscores the word's role as a personal identifier within the apostolic list, emphasizing the historical reality of this individual among Jesus' chosen twelve.
theologicalSignificance: Though the name Θαδδαῖος itself does not carry a known root meaning, its presence as one of the twelve apostles holds significant theological weight. Thaddaeus represents the faithful witnesses chosen by Christ to carry the gospel forward, highlighting the personal calling and distinct roles within the apostolic mission. Recognizing him by name affirms the concrete historical foundation of the New Testament witness and the diverse individuals God used to establish the early church. His inclusion reminds believers that every apostle, known by name, was integral to the fulfillment of Christ's redemptive plan.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 10:3, the apostle list includes 'Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus,' linking two names to one person. This verse situates Θαδδαῖος within the intimate circle of Jesus' chosen messengers, emphasizing his identity and role. The use of Θαδδαῖος here clarifies the apostle's name and affirms his place among those sent by Christ, encouraging believers to remember the personal and relational nature of the apostolic commission.
